```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# Every chunk on this page runs from the root of the site, whose data/ folder
# holds the same files as that of the workspace, so that the paths read exactly
# as they do in the workspace and in the browser lab: data/housing_emails.csv.
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = "..")
```

```{r}
#| label: page-numbers
#| include: false
# The numbers quoted in the prose, computed from the curve of the case study.
page_curve <- readr::read_csv("data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
ref_row    <- page_curve |> datawizard::data_filter(is_reference)
ref_gap    <- insight::format_value(ref_row$b_pp, digits = 2, style_negative = "minus")
```

The specifications of the exercise in the Housing and racial bias case study are fitted with helper functions, which are introduced here. The page assumes the R taught in [Getting started with R](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r.html), the module on the workshop's umbrella website, written on the data of this case study, up to [section 10](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r.html#sec-shares), in which the share of replies that greeted the sender by name is computed for two groups of names and the difference between the two shares is taken.

The code on this page ran when the page was built, and what R printed appears under each block, which allows you to compare your own output with the page line by line. Type each block into the [workspace](../tracks/day/before.qmd#the-workspace) that you downloaded, or, if your installation fails, into the [browser lab](../lab.qmd), where the helpers are already loaded.

## A first look at `try_spec()` {#sec-try-spec}

The workspace holds a file of helper functions, `R/spec_tools.R`, which the exercise loads once and then uses to fit specifications. A **specification** is one complete set of choices for an analysis, fixing which names are compared, which emails are counted, what happens to the uncoded replies, which model is fitted and which covariates it includes. `source()` runs the file and makes its functions available in your session. In the browser lab the helpers are already loaded, and the line is not needed.

```{r}
#| label: source-tools
#| eval: false
source("R/spec_tools.R")
```

```{r}
#| label: source-tools-page
#| include: false
# The page reads the helpers from the local copy of the workspace, the
# repository ar4ds-housing-workspace in the folder beside this repository, and its
# data/ from the root of the site, which holds the same files.
source("../ar4ds-housing-workspace/R/spec_tools.R")
```

`try_spec()` fits one specification and prints its result. Every argument has a default, the defaults together making up the reference specification, the comparison made by hand in section 10 of Getting started with R, and calling the function with no arguments therefore reproduces the gap computed there:

```{r}
#| label: try-reference
try_spec()
```

The first lines repeat the two shares and their difference, `r ref_gap` points, now with a 95% interval around it. The test line comes from a linear probability model, explained in the [binary-outcomes module](binary-outcomes.qmd), which regresses the 0/1 outcome on an indicator of the Hispanic names and whose coefficient is exactly the difference in shares. The last lines give the number of replies analysed, a partial correlation computed by the rule used in the SCORE robustness study (Aczel et al. 2026), the class of the result, and its place among the `r nrow(page_curve)` specifications on the curve of the claim.

Changing one argument changes one decision, and `population = "all"`, for instance, counts every delivered email, as the second calculation of that section does:

```{r}
#| label: try-all
try_spec(population = "all")
```

Options that are not on the curve are refused, with the reason and the page on the workshop's website on which they are taught. In the call below the outcome is set to any reply instead of a greeting by name, which would answer a different claim:

```{r}
#| label: try-refused
#| error: true
try_spec(outcome = "reply")
```

Every call to `try_spec()` is logged, and `my_experiments()` prints the log, showing only the decisions that you varied:

```{r}
#| label: my-experiments
my_experiments()
```

These steps amount to the whole of Task 4 in miniature, in which you change one decision at a time, read what moves and keep a record. The [specification menu](../menu.qmd) lists every argument and its options, while the [cheatsheet](../cheatsheet.qmd) gathers the helpers on one page.
